story: Five lakes lie in a chain along a narrow valley in Hawkesbury sandstone: Lake Gandangarra, Lake Werri Berri, Lake Couridjah, Lake Baraba and Lake Nerrigorang. Sandstone slopes from the east and west meet to form Blue Gum Creek, and its water flows into the lakes. They are shallow, and they lose water both by evaporation and by leaking into the ground beneath their sediments. They are thought to be about 15 million years old.

The lakes have always come and gone. Sediment cores show a long dry spell about 12,000 to 21,000 years ago, and records from the past 120 years show the lakes drying out from time to time. They fell sharply in the Millennium Drought of 2001 to 2010 and again in the drought that began in 2017. Local people feared the cause was nearby coal mining. A government research program from 2017 to 2021 found that climate variability caused an estimated 83 to 98 per cent of the change in water levels. It found no direct link to the mine, but could not rule out a smaller effect. Heavy rain in 2020, 2021 and 2022 brought the lakes back to perhaps their highest levels in a decade.

The lakes lie where Dharug, Tharawal and Gundungurra lands meet. They are important places for cultural practice and for Aboriginal custodians' connection to Country. The water draws a remarkable range of birds: more than 140 species, including white-faced herons, musk ducks, Pacific black ducks, pied cormorants, Australasian grebes and white-bellied sea eagles.

In the steam age the lakes worked for the railway. A sandstone pump station on the shore of Lake Couridjah sent water up to Couridjah station, where steam locomotives on the old southern line refilled their tanks. The restored pump house and the pump keeper's track survive. The area was first reserved in 1972 as Thirlmere Lakes State Park, later became a national park, and in 2000 joined the Greater Blue Mountains World Heritage Area, the smallest of its eight reserves.
howItWorks: Thirlmere Lakes is run by the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS). Of the state's more than 890 parks and reserves, 45 charge a vehicle entry fee. Thirlmere Lakes is listed among them, but NPWS says entry is under review and no fee is being collected. The annual All Parks Pass, $190 a year as listed by NPWS in November 2026, covers vehicle entry to every fee-collecting park in NSW, including Kosciuszko. The Multi Park Pass covers all of them except Kosciuszko for $65.

The park is a day-use area, open from 5.30 am to 8 pm during daylight saving and to 6 pm the rest of the year. It may close in poor weather or high fire danger. NPWS lists no campground here, so for an overnight stay look in the nearby Wollondilly towns or in the other Blue Mountains parks. You can swim and paddle in the lakes when there is enough water, but not when levels are low.

Bushfire season runs from October to March. On total fire ban days, usually declared around 5 pm the day before, every wood or solid-fuel fire and barbecue is prohibited in NSW parks, as are liquid-fuel stoves. NPWS-installed gas barbecues may still be used under supervision, with nothing that can burn within two metres and water at hand. NPWS can also declare a park fire ban, or close the park when the fire risk to visitors is high, so check NPWS alerts before you go.

camping: NPWS lists no campground in the park
lodging: Accommodation in Picton, Thirlmere and the other Wollondilly towns
seasonalClosures: No seasonal closure. The park is open 5.30 am to 8 pm in daylight saving and to 6 pm otherwise, and may close in poor weather or high fire danger — check NPWS alerts before you go

chronology.text: The lakes are thought to have formed.
A long dry period is recorded in the lakes' sediments.
Thirlmere Lakes State Park is reserved in March; it becomes a national park in 1974.
The park is inscribed with seven other reserves as the Greater Blue Mountains Area World Heritage property.
After years of falling water, an inquiry is held into the lakes' levels and possible mining or groundwater impacts.
The NSW Government commits $1.9 million to a four-year Thirlmere Lakes Research Program with UNSW, the University of Wollongong and ANSTO.
A synthesis of the research is published; it names climate variability as the main driver of the lakes' drying.

safety: Do not swim or paddle when the lake levels are low.
Mobile reception is limited. In an emergency call Triple Zero (000); the Emergency Plus app gives your location.
The lakes walking track has no directional signs. Carry a map and enough water.
Check NPWS alerts and the Rural Fire Service before you go: the park may close on days of high fire danger.
regulations: No pets or domestic animals, except certified assistance animals.
No smoking: NSW national parks are smoke-free.
No wood or solid-fuel fires during total fire bans or park fire bans.
Day use only; the park closes at 8 pm in daylight saving and at 6 pm the rest of the year.

weather: Summer days average 14°C to 28°C and have reached 42.8°C. Winter averages 2°C to 17°C, and nights can be bitter: the record low is −10°C. Frost and mist on the lakes on winter mornings make this a good season for photographs. March is usually the wettest month and September the driest. In spring the ground orchids flower and the birds are at their busiest.
directions: The park is a short drive from Picton, south-west of Sydney. From Picton, follow Remembrance Drive south, turn right onto Thirlmere Way and then right onto Richardson Street. Veer left at Westbourne Avenue and continue along Barbour Road into the park. From Bargo, head north-west on Remembrance Drive, turn left at Tahmoor onto Bargo River Road, then turn right at Couridjah onto West Parade. NPWS advises that the park cannot be reached by public transport.
